claim: The average success rate of in vitro fertilization (IVF) in the US was approximately 30% in 2015.
source: Assisted reproductive technologies (ART) such as in vitro fertilization (IVF), while a solution to many infertile couples have been inefficient with an average success rate of approximately 30% reported in 2015 in the US (CDC, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to CDC, 2015 data.

claim: IVF costs patients well over $10,000 out-of-pocket for each ART cycle in the US.
source: IVF is also an expensive solution costing patients well over $10,000 out-of-pocket for each ART cycle in the US with many patients requiring multiple cycles to achieve successful pregnancy (CDC, 2015; Birenbaum-Carmeli, 2004; Toner, 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to CDC, 2015; Birenbaum-Carmeli, 2004; Toner, 2002.

claim: Many IVF patients require multiple cycles to achieve successful pregnancy.
source: IVF is also an expensive solution costing patients well over $10,000 out-of-pocket for each ART cycle in the US with many patients requiring multiple cycles to achieve successful pregnancy (CDC, 2015; Birenbaum-Carmeli, 2004; Toner, 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to CDC, 2015; Birenbaum-Carmeli, 2004; Toner, 2002.

claim: Non-invasive selection of the highest quality embryo for transfer is one of the most important factors in achieving successful ART outcomes.
source: Although multiple factors such as maternal age, medical diagnosis, gamete and embryo quality, and endometrium receptivity determine the success of ART cycles, the challenge of non-invasive selection of the highest available quality from a patient's cohort of embryos (top-quality embryo) for transfer remains as one of the most important factors in achieving successful ART outcomes (Vaegter et al., 2017; Barash et al., 2017; Conaghan et al., 2013; Wong et al., 2013; Racowsky et al., 2015; Filho et al., 2010; Machtinger and Racowsky, 2013; Demko et al., 2016; Einarsson et al., 2017; Hill et al., 1989; Erenus et al., 1991; Paulson et al., 1990; Osman et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Traditional methods of embryo selection rely on visual embryo morphological assessment and are highly practice-dependent and subjective.
source: Traditional methods of embryo selection rely on visual embryo morphological assessment and are highly practice-dependent and subjective (Storr et al., 2017; Baxter Bendus et al., 2006; Paternot et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Storr et al., 2017; Baxter Bendus et al., 2006; Paternot et al., 2009.

claim: Fully automated assessments of embryos are challenging owing to the complexity of embryo morphologies.
source: Fully automated assessments of embryos are challenging owing to the complexity of embryo morphologies.
evidence: The claim is based on general knowledge about the complexity of embryo morphologies.

claim: Emulating the skill of highly trained embryologists in efficient embryo assessment in a fully automated system is a major challenge in previous computer-aided assessments of embryos.
source: Emulating the skill of highly trained embryologists in efficient embryo assessment in a fully automated system is a major challenge in all of the previous work done in computer-aided assessments of embryos due to focus on measuring specific expert-defined parameters such as zona pellucida thickness variation, number of blastomeres, degree of cell symmetry and cytoplasmic fragmentation, etc. (Rocha et al., 2017a; Rocha et al., 2017b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Rocha et al., 2017a; Rocha et al., 2017b.

claim: Most fertility centers do not possess time-lapse imaging hardware even in the United States of America.
source: It is important to emphasize here that most fertility centers do not possess time-lapse imaging hardware even in the United States of America (Dolinko et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Dolinko et al., 2017.

claim: Blastocyst embryo transfers have been associated with better implantation rates.
source: Blastocyst embryo transfers, in particular, have been associated with better implantation rates and have helped lower the number of embryos transferred at a time (De Croo et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to De Croo et al., 2019.

claim: Blastocyst embryo transfers have helped lower the number of embryos transferred at a time.
source: Blastocyst embryo transfers, in particular, have been associated with better implantation rates and have helped lower the number of embryos transferred at a time (De Croo et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to De Croo et al., 2019.

claim: A CNN trained using 2440 static human embryo images recorded at 113 hr post insemination was used to develop neural networks for identifying embryos capable of implantation.
source: Therefore, in this study, we have investigated the use of a CNN pre-trained with 1.4 million ImageNet images and transfer-learned using 2440 static human embryo images recorded at a single time-point of 113 hr post insemination (hpi) for the development of neural networks that can help identify embryos capable of implantation and for identifying the top quality embryos (Figure 1).
evidence: The claim describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: The CNN was pre-trained with 1.4 million ImageNet images.
source: Therefore, in this study, we have investigated the use of a CNN pre-trained with 1.4 million ImageNet images and transfer-learned using 2440 static human embryo images recorded at a single time-point of 113 hr post insemination (hpi) for the development of neural networks that can help identify embryos capable of implantation and for identifying the top quality embryos (Figure 1).
evidence: The claim describes the pre-training methodology used in the study.

claim: The CNN achieved 90% accuracy in choosing the highest quality embryo available from 97 clinical patient cohorts (742 embryos).
source: Here, we evaluated the use of a deep convolutional neural network (CNN), trained using single timepoint images of embryos collected at 113 hr post-insemination, in embryo selection amongst 97 clinical patient cohorts (742 embryos) and observed an accuracy of 90% in choosing the highest quality embryo available.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: A CNN trained to assess an embryo's implantation potential directly using 97 euploid embryos outperformed 15 trained embryologists (75.26% vs. 67.35%, p<0.0001).
source: Furthermore, a CNN trained to assess an embryo's implantation potential directly using a set of 97 euploid embryos capable of implantation outperformed 15 trained embryologists (75.26% vs. 67.35%, p<0.0001) from five different fertility centers.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing CNN and embryologist performance.

claim: The neural network performed with an accuracy of 90.97% (area under the curve: 0.96) in differentiating between blastocysts and non-blastocysts (n = 742).
source: In our evaluations of the CNN in categorizing embryos imaged at 113 hpi based on their morphology, the network performed with an accuracy of 90.97% (area under the curve: 0.96) in differentiating between blastocysts and non-blastocysts (n = 742) (Kanakasabapathy et al., 2019a; Thirumalaraju et al., 2020; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and references Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The CNNg algorithm performed with an accuracy of 98.96% for single embryo transfer (SET) in selecting blastocysts at 113 hpi.
source: For blastocyst selections at 113 hpi, the CNNg algorithm performed with an accuracy of 98.96% for SET, which was similar (p>0.05) to the average accuracy of the embryologists (96.91%, CI: 94.69% to 99.12%) (n = 5) (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and references Figure 2A.

claim: The CNNg algorithm's accuracy for SET in selecting blastocysts was similar (p>0.05) to the average accuracy of embryologists (96.91%, CI: 94.69% to 99.12%).
source: For blastocyst selections at 113 hpi, the CNNg algorithm performed with an accuracy of 98.96% for SET, which was similar (p>0.05) to the average accuracy of the embryologists (96.91%, CI: 94.69% to 99.12%) (n = 5) (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical comparison of experimental data.

claim: The CNNg algorithm performed with an accuracy of 100.00% for double embryo transfer (DET) in selecting blastocysts.
source: However, when two embryo selections for DET were allowed based on blastocyst and non-blastocyst classification, the CNNg algorithm performed with an accuracy of 100.00%, which was better (p<0.05) than embryologists (n = 5) who performed with an average accuracy of 98.76% (CI: 97.69% to 99.83%) (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and references Figure 2B.

claim: The CNNg algorithm's accuracy for DET in selecting blastocysts was better (p<0.05) than embryologists who performed with an average accuracy of 98.76% (CI: 97.69% to 99.83%).
source: However, when two embryo selections for DET were allowed based on blastocyst and non-blastocyst classification, the CNNg algorithm performed with an accuracy of 100.00%, which was better (p<0.05) than embryologists (n = 5) who performed with an average accuracy of 98.76% (CI: 97.69% to 99.83%) (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical comparison of experimental data.

claim: The accuracy of the CNNg algorithm for SET in selecting the highest quality blastocysts at 113 hpi was 89.69%.
source: Toward the selection of HQB at 113 hpi, the accuracy of the CNNg algorithm for SET was 89.69% similar (p>0.05) to the embryologists (n = 5) who performed with an average accuracy of 90.31% (CI: 87.50% to 93.11%) (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and references Figure 2C.

claim: The CNNg algorithm's accuracy for SET in selecting highest quality blastocysts was similar (p>0.05) to embryologists who performed with an average accuracy of 90.31% (CI: 87.50% to 93.11%).
source: Toward the selection of HQB at 113 hpi, the accuracy of the CNNg algorithm for SET was 89.69% similar (p>0.05) to the embryologists (n = 5) who performed with an average accuracy of 90.31% (CI: 87.50% to 93.11%) (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical comparison of experimental data.

claim: The CNNg algorithm performed with an accuracy of 97.94% for DET in selecting highest quality blastocysts at 113 hpi.
source: When two embryo selections for DET at 113 hpi were allowed, the system performed with a better (p<0.05) accuracy of 97.94% in comparison to the embryologists who performed with an average accuracy of 96.91% (CI: 96.00% to 97.81%) (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and references Figure 2D.

claim: The CNNg algorithm's accuracy for DET in selecting highest quality blastocysts was better (p<0.05) than embryologists who performed with an average accuracy of 96.91% (CI: 96.00% to 97.81%).
source: When two embryo selections for DET at 113 hpi were allowed, the system performed with a better (p<0.05) accuracy of 97.94% in comparison to the embryologists who performed with an average accuracy of 96.91% (CI: 96.00% to 97.81%) (Figure 2D).
